definition: A common contraction of 'para allá'. In Caribbean and urban Spanish dialects, the 'ara' is often elided in speech. In this context, it is used to dismiss negative energy or bad vibes, literally telling them to go 'over there'.

An idiomatic expression of extreme self-confidence. While it literally translates to 'I go to me,' it means 'I believe in myself' or 'I am betting on my own success' regardless of the odds or others' opinions.

example.spanish: Y yo voy a mí (a mí)
example.english: And I believe in myself (in myself)

definition: A frequent phonetic contraction of 'todo' (all/every) where the 'd' is dropped. This is a hallmark of urban music and regional Caribbean accents, representing how the language is actually spoken in the streets versus how it is written.
While 'dieta' usually refers to nutrition, here it is used as a humorous metaphor. Saying a wallet is 'on a diet' means it is thin or empty because it lacks money (the 'fat').

example.spanish: Que mi cartera no haga más dieta
example.english: Let my wallet stop its diet

definition: The verb 'virarse' means to turn or flip. In a social or karmic context, it implies that one's actions will eventually turn around and hit them back, or that someone might 'turn' on you (betrayal).

example.spanish: No hagas el mal porque todo se te vira
example.english: Don’t do evil because it all turns back on you

definition: A phrase used to describe people who gossip, lie, or speak ill of others. In many Latin cultures, 'malas lenguas' are viewed as a source of negative energy or bad luck that one must protect themselves from.

example.spanish: Que la mala lengua no tenga chance
example.english: Let the wicked tongue have no chance

definition: A direct loanword (anglicism) from English. While 'oportunidad' is the formal term, 'chance' is used extensively in informal Spanish to mean a break, a possibility, or an opening.

example.spanish: Que la mala lengua no tenga chance
example.english: Let the wicked tongue have no chance
